questions.text: What is CSS and what is its purpose?

answers.content: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is a stylesheet language used to describe the presentation and layout of document markup (HTML).

questions.text:
What is the difference between
,
, and
semantic elements?

answers.content: represents a thematic grouping of content, typically with a heading.
represents a self-contained, independent composition (e.g., blog post).
represents tangential or sidebar content related to the surrounding context.

questions.text: What is the difference between block and inline HTML elements?

answers.content: Block elements start on a new line and take up the full width of the container.
Inline elements do not start on a new line and only take up the width necessary for their content.

questions.text: What is the CSS opacity property and its valid range?

answers.content: Opacity specifies the transparency of an element. Its valid range is 0.0 (fully transparent) to 1.0 (fully opaque).

questions.text: How does Flexbox differ from Grid? When would you use one over the other?

answers.content: Flexbox is designed for one-dimensional layouts (either a row or a column).
Grid is designed for two-dimensional layouts (both rows and columns simultaneously).

questions.text: What are the different ways to center elements horizontally and vertically (e.g., Flexbox, margin: auto, text-align)?

answers.content: Flexbox: display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;
Grid: display: grid; place-items: center;
Absolute: position: absolute; top: 50%; left: 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%);

questions.text: Difference between absolute, relative, fixed, static, and sticky CSS positioning.

answers.content: static: Default layout flow.
relative: Positioned relative to its normal flow position.
absolute: Positioned relative to its nearest non-static positioned ancestor.
fixed: Positioned relative to the viewport.
sticky: Hybrid positioning toggling between relative and fixed based on scroll offsets.

questions.text: How does the CSS box model impact layouts, and what role does box-sizing play?

answers.content: The box model wraps elements in content, padding, border, and margin.
box-sizing: content-box (default) adds padding and borders on top of width/height.
box-sizing: border-box absorbs padding and borders inside width/height.

questions.text: Difference between display: none and visibility: hidden.

answers.content: display: none hides the element and removes it from the document flow (takes up no space).
visibility: hidden hides the element but preserves its space in the layout.

questions.text: What is CSS Specificity? How does the browser calculate style priority?

answers.content: A weight system determining which CSS rules apply: Inline styles > IDs > Classes/Pseudo-classes > Elements/Pseudo-elements.

questions.text: What is the difference between pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements?

answers.content: Pseudo-classes select states of an element (e.g., :hover, :focus).
Pseudo-elements style specific parts of an element (e.g., ::before, ::after).

questions.text: How do you make a website responsive across different devices?

answers.content: Using CSS media queries, responsive grids (Flexbox/Grid), and fluid units (%, vw, vh, rem, em).

questions.text: What are some of the latest CSS features/properties introduced recently?

answers.content: CSS Nesting, @container queries, :has() relational selector, subgrid, and new color spaces (oklch).

questions.text: Which libraries or frameworks have you used for writing CSS?

answers.content: Tailwind CSS, Styled Components (CSS-in-JS), SASS/SCSS, CSS Modules.

questions.text: If you were building a complete website like Amazon or Myntra from scratch, would you use Flexbox or Grid? Why?

answers.content: A hybrid approach: Grid for high-level main structures (header, content columns, footer grids) and Flexbox for nested, one-dimensional dynamic layouts (navbar links, card contents).

questions.text: How do you handle cross-browser quirks without breaking the user experience?

answers.content: Feature queries (@supports), CSS resets/normalizers, autoprefixer compilation plugins, and robust fallback styles.

questions.text: If you have a 2MB image, how would you efficiently display it across all responsive devices?

answers.content: Compress via modern formats (webp, avif), utilize CDN imaging optimization APIs, lazy-load (loading="lazy"), and implement srcset on wrappers.

questions.text: How does browser rendering work internally (repaint, reflow, compositing) and what causes UI jank?

answers.content: Reflow recalculates layout dimensions. Repaint redraws pixels. Compositing layers elements. Jank occurs when main thread execution lags, dropping frames below 60fps.

questions.text: Explain what happens internally from a network and browser perspective when a user types a URL in the browser and hits Enter.

answers.content: DNS resolution converts domain to IP. TCP handshake establishes connection. TLS negotiation secures it. HTTP request fetches resource. HTML is parsed, constructing DOM/CSSOM. Layout and paint phases render the pixels.

questions.text: What is the difference between null, undefined, and NaN?

answers.content: null: Explicit assignment representing the intentional absence of value.
undefined: Declared variable that hasn't been assigned a value.
NaN: Not-a-Number, representing numeric computational failures.

questions.text: What is hoisting? Explain the concept of hoisting with an example.

answers.content: Declarations are moved to the top of their enclosing scope prior to script execution.
Code:

answers.code:
console.log(x); // undefined
     var x = 5;

questions.text: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) in JavaScript?

answers.content: The state between variable binding creation and its declaration line (using let or const) where variable access throws a ReferenceError.

questions.text: Explain the difference between var, let, and const. When should each be used?

answers.content: var is function-scoped and hoisted with undefined.
let is block-scoped and hoisted into the TDZ.
const is block-scoped, hoisted into the TDZ, and requires read-only value binding initialization.

questions.text: What is the difference between == and ===? Why is strict equality generally preferred?

answers.content: == performs type coercion before comparison. === compares values and types strictly. Strict equality prevents hidden type bugs.

questions.text: What is callback hell, and how can it be avoided?

answers.content: Excessive nesting of callback handlers causing unreadable "pyramid of doom" patterns. Avoided using Promises or async/await.

questions.text: Difference between synchronous and asynchronous JavaScript.

answers.content: Synchronous runs line-by-line in a blocking thread. Asynchronous registers callbacks or promises to handle tasks in a non-blocking queue.

questions.text: What is the difference between map(), filter(), forEach(), and reduce()?

answers.content: map() returns a transformed array.
filter() returns elements matching conditions.
forEach() iterates over items returning undefined.
reduce() aggregates elements to a single value.

questions.text: Difference between normal functions and arrow functions.

answers.content: Arrow functions capture lexical scope this values, cannot act as constructors, lack an arguments object, and cannot act as generator functions.

questions.text: Explain Objects in JavaScript. What types of Objects are there, and how do you define them?

answers.content: Collections of key-value pairs. Built-in types include arrays, functions, dates, regExps. Defined via literal, constructors, or Object.create().

questions.text: What is the difference between the spread (...) operator and the rest (...) operator?

answers.content: Spread expands collections into individual components. Rest accumulates multiple items into a single container array/object.

questions.text: What are the key ES6 features in JavaScript?

answers.content: Classes, template literals, destructuring, promises, modules, default parameters, map/set collections.

questions.text: What is the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?

answers.content: localStorage data persists indefinitely. sessionStorage clears as soon as the browsing session or tab is closed.

questions.text: Explain closures in JavaScript and how they can be used to implement private variables.

answers.content: Closures form when nested functions capture references to outer scope variables. Capturing prevents outer execution garbage collection.

questions.text: How do call(), apply(), and bind() differ? Can they be used with Arrow Functions?

answers.content: call() runs function specifying this and individual arguments.
apply() runs function specifying this and array argument.
bind() returns function binding this.
They cannot override this on arrow functions since arrow functions capture this lexically.

questions.text: Explain prototypal inheritance and the prototype chain.

answers.content: Objects inherit methods from parent prototypes linked via double-underscore references, searching upwards until null.

questions.text: What is event delegation, and why is it useful in large DOM trees?

answers.content: Single parent element handles events bubbling up from descendants, saving memory allocation costs.

questions.text: Event bubbling vs capturing — where have you applied this in production?

answers.content: Bubbling triggers from child to parent. Capturing runs parent down to child. Applied in global analytics listeners.

questions.text: What is the difference between a Deep Copy and a Shallow Copy? How can you clone nested objects?

answers.content: Shallow copy references nested pointers. Deep copy duplicates recursive levels. Clone via structuredClone() or libraries.

questions.text: What is a Promise in JavaScript? How do Promises differ from async/await?

answers.content: Promises represent eventual async success/failure. async/await is cleaner syntax built on top of Promise resolvers.

questions.text: How do you handle asynchronous operations using async/await?

answers.content: Using async function blocks wrapping await triggers inside try/catch sequences.

questions.text: What are higher-order functions? Name some built-in JavaScript methods that use them.

answers.content: Functions accepting or returning other functions (e.g. map, filter, reduce).

questions.text: Explain the JavaScript execution context, lexical scope, and call stack.

answers.content: The environment executing code is context. Lexical scope sets variable boundaries based on placement. Call stack manages contexts.

questions.text: Explain CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) in simple terms.

answers.content: Browser safety protocol restricting client cross-origin headers unless permitted by target servers.

questions.text: Explain the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies in terms of security and scalability.

answers.content: Storage holds 5-10MB. Cookies hold 4KB and travel on HTTP requests, raising vulnerabilities unless flag attributes (Secure, HttpOnly) are configured.

questions.text: What is the JavaScript event loop? Explain microtasks, macrotasks, and the callback queue with examples.

answers.content: Orchestrator prioritizing call stack clearance before microtasks (Promises) and macrotasks (setTimeout callbacks).

questions.text: Why does the event loop matter for performance-heavy applications?

answers.content: Blocking the execution context stack prevents the event loop from rendering, dropping frames and freezing user interactions.

questions.text: What is Garbage Collection in JavaScript, and how does it work?

answers.content: Reclaims memory allocated to unreachable variables using a mark-and-sweep reference algorithm.

questions.text: What is Currying? Implement sum(1)(2)(3) in JavaScript.

answers.content: Currying splits a multi-parameter function into single-parameter functions.
Code:

answers.code: const sum = a => b => c => a + b + c;

questions.text: Explain race conditions in frontend applications.

answers.content: Async responses return in unpredictable order, updating state incorrectly. Resolved using cancellation hooks or abort controls.

questions.text: How would you optimize a JavaScript application that becomes slow with large datasets?

answers.content: Use pagination, virtualized viewports, custom indexing web-workers, and debounce high-frequency calculations.

questions.text: Explain browser caching strategies with examples.

answers.content: Service worker cache-first, network-first, Cache-Control headers (max-age, must-revalidate, no-cache, ETag validation).

questions.text: What is TypeScript and how does it differ from JavaScript?

answers.content: A typed compiler superset of JavaScript providing compile-time checks and type annotations.

questions.text: Difference between type and interface in TypeScript. When would you choose one over the other?

answers.content: Interfaces allow decoration merges. Types support unions, aliases, and primitives. Choose interfaces for extensible API schemas.

questions.text: Explain TypeScript interfaces, types, enums, and when to use each.

answers.content: Interfaces check object structures. Types create complex signatures. Enums declare fixed sets of named numerical or string constants.

questions.text: Explain TypeScript utility types like Partial, Pick, Omit, Exclude, and Record.

answers.content: Partial makes fields optional. Pick selects subset parameters. Omit ignores attributes. Exclude filters types. Record creates key-value maps.

questions.text: How does TypeScript's Generics feature help in large-scale applications?

answers.content: Builds scalable, type-safe API abstractions and data-structures that support varying inputs without writing duplicate models.

questions.text: What are mapped types, keyof, keyof typeof, and conditional types in TypeScript?

answers.content: Mapped types modify structural attributes. keyof lists object keys. Conditional types select signatures dynamically based on checks.

questions.text: What is React?

answers.content: A declarative component library designed for building dynamic UI views.

questions.text: What is a React element vs a React component?

answers.content: Elements are simple objects describing DOM configurations. Components are functions or classes returning elements.

questions.text: What is JSX? How does Babel compile JSX?

answers.content: HTML-like syntax compiled into React.createElement() method calls.

questions.text: What is the difference between React and ReactDOM?

answers.content: React manages components and Virtual DOM layouts. ReactDOM translates virtual representations to web DOM components.

questions.text: What is the Virtual DOM? Why is React faster than traditional DOM manipulation?

answers.content: In-memory representations mapped to real views. Diff calculations minimize real DOM repaints and reflow calculations.

questions.text: Difference between functional and class components.

answers.content: Functional components are simple functions using hooks. Class components are ES6 classes managing lifecycles.

questions.text: What are props vs state? Difference between state and props?

answers.content: State is mutable local memory. Props are immutable parameters received from parent scopes.

questions.text: Explain parent-to-child and child-to-parent component communication.

answers.content: Parents pass data to children via props. Children invoke passed callback functions to pass data back.

questions.text: What is state lifting in React?

answers.content: Extracting shared states to the closest common parent node.

questions.text: What are default props?

answers.content: Predefined fallback prop attributes used if parent allocations are omitted.

questions.text: What are the conditional rendering techniques in React? How do you show and hide components conditionally?

answers.content: Ternaries, logic execution filters (&&), and inline returns.

questions.text: How do you loop over arrays and objects in React?

answers.content: map() for arrays, Object.keys() or Object.entries() iteration maps for objects.

questions.text: How do you change styles dynamically based on conditions?

answers.content: Using conditional inline styles or template string calculations on className attributes.

questions.text: How do you display user‑entered data in another textbox?

answers.content: Synchronize inputs by mapping change triggers to a shared parent hook state.

questions.text: How does React's reconciliation algorithm and Virtual DOM diffing work?

answers.content: An algorithm that calculates component element changes, utilizing keys for performance and matching type boundaries.

questions.text: What is prop drilling, and how do you avoid it in a large application?

answers.content: Passing props deep. Avoided using Context API, custom hooks, or state managers.

questions.text: Why are keys important in dynamic rendering? Explain React's reconciliation process and the role of keys.

answers.content: Keys preserve component identities during lists updates, avoiding slow reconstruction of identical DOM structures.

questions.text: How do you display dynamic HTML data in React?

answers.content: By wrapping content in dangerouslySetInnerHTML attributes.

questions.text: How do you bind an array or object list to a dropdown, display the selected value elsewhere, and handle dependent dropdowns (e.g., country to state)?

answers.content: Render state-driven select options, matching changes to separate list filter hooks.

questions.text: How do you bind radio buttons using an array of objects and display the selected radio value in another field?

answers.content: Match radio selections to state variables and render selections using secondary text parameters.

questions.text: What are React Hooks? Explain the main built-in hooks.

answers.content: Functions providing hooks into states and lifecycles. Key hooks: useState, useEffect, useContext, useRef.

questions.text: Explain the useState hook.

answers.content: Returns a state container state value and a state setter.

questions.text: Explain the useEffect hook and the cleanup function.

answers.content: Runs side effects. Cleanup functions clear registers prior to unmounting or execution updates.

questions.text: What are the different dependency array scenarios in useEffect?

answers.content: Omitted: runs on every paint. []: runs on mount. [deps]: runs when values in deps update.

questions.text: How do you call a method when a component mounts for the first time?

answers.content: Trigger within useEffect using empty array dependencies.

questions.text: Replace class lifecycle methods using useEffect.

questions.text: Explain the useContext hook.

questions.text: How do you access and manipulate a DOM element using useRef?

answers.content: Bind the ref object to the element and access it via ref.current.

questions.text: How do useEffect dependencies work under the hood? What are some common mistakes developers make?

answers.content: Shallow comparisons. Mistakes include omitting values, causing infinite loops.

questions.text: If useEffect and useMemo have the same dependency array, which executes first and why?

answers.content: useMemo runs first during rendering. useEffect runs asynchronously after layout/paint cycles.

questions.text: Why does useEffect run twice in Strict Mode?

answers.content: Verifies that cleanup effects are properly established.

questions.text: Can we use Hooks inside conditions? Why?

answers.content: No. Breaking call orders breaks the hook indexing map.

questions.text: Explain the useRef hook in depth. How is it different from useState? When would you use useRef instead of useState?

answers.content: useRef modifications do not trigger re-renders. Use to reference DOM nodes or compile persist values.

questions.text: Explain useMemo and provide an example of optimization.

answers.content: Memoizes values.
Code:

answers.code: const calc = useMemo(() => heavyMath(x), [x]);

questions.text: Explain useCallback and provide an example of optimization.

answers.content: Memoizes references to callbacks.
Code:

answers.code: const handle = useCallback(() => click(id), [id]);

questions.text: Difference between useMemo and useCallback. When would you use each?

answers.content: useMemo resolves return objects. useCallback preserves callback references.

questions.text: Explain the useReducer hook.

answers.content: Manages complex state changes through a reducer function.

questions.text: When should you create Custom Hooks? Why do we use them, and how do they improve code reusability?

answers.content: Extract custom sequences to hooks to prevent duplication.

questions.text: Explain the useDeferredValue hook and its use cases.

answers.content: Defers rendering expensive components until critical cycles finish.

questions.text: Explain the useTransition hook and concurrent rendering.

answers.content: Splits states into low-priority transitions.

questions.text: What is the difference between useEffect and useLayoutEffect?

answers.content: useLayoutEffect runs before browser paints. useEffect runs after paint.

questions.text: Explain useImperativeHandle and how it works with forwardRef.

answers.content: Customizes ref values returned to parent scopes.

questions.text: Explain stale closures in React. What are they, and how are they used inside React hooks?

answers.content: Closures referencing outdated scope objects due to missing dependencies.

questions.text: How does React schedule effects?

answers.content: Runs them in async processes scheduled after paint.

questions.text: Explain the React component lifecycle and how hooks map to lifecycle phases.

answers.content: Lifecycle phases: Mount, Update, Unmount. mapped to useEffect dependencies.

questions.text: How do you run logic after a state update or re‑render? How do you execute logic on every re‑render?

answers.content: Match deps to trigger useEffect after rendering. Use no deps to trigger on every paint cycle.

questions.text: Create controlled vs uncontrolled components. What is the difference between them?

answers.content: Controlled: values bound to state. Uncontrolled: values accessed via DOM hooks.

questions.text: What are the different form validation approaches in React?

answers.content: Form-level hooks state checks, or custom libraries (yup, zod).

questions.text: How do you handle multiple input fields in a React form?

questions.text: What is Context API? Have you used Context API?

questions.text: What is debouncing and throttling? Where have you used them in production?

questions.text: Explain React Architecture.

answers.content: React architecture is structured around components, unidirectional data flow, reconciliation, rendering, and lifecycle states.

questions.text: Can React Hooks completely replace Redux? When should you still use a state management library?

answers.content: No, Hooks (Context API) are not built for high-frequency updates and lack structural middleware or devtool features.

questions.text: If useEffect and useMemo have the same dependency array, which executes first and why?

answers.content: useMemo runs first during rendering. useEffect runs asynchronously after layout and paint phases are complete.

questions.text: Tell me about your React Native experience and project history.

answers.content: Be prepared to discuss cross-platform deployments, native module integrations, JSI bridges, and mmkv/sqlite local cache setups.

questions.text: What challenges did you face, and how did you resolve production crashes?

questions.text: Explain closures with a real-world analogy.

answers.content: Analogous to a backpack that a hiking guide carries. The guide is the function, and the gear in the backpack is the lexical scope variables that travel with the function.

questions.text: When would you actually use == over ===?

answers.content: Rarely. Used only when you want to compare if a value is loosely null/undefined (e.g., x == null checks if x is null or undefined).

questions.text: If you have a 2MB image, how would you efficiently display it across all responsive devices?

answers.content: Compress the image, serve responsive sizes using srcset/picture elements, lazy load, and utilize a CDN.

questions.text: If you were building a complete website like Amazon from scratch, would you use Flexbox or Grid? Why?

answers.content: Both. Grid for page-level layouts (header, main container, footer) and Flexbox for one-dimensional components (navbar items, product cards).

answers.content: Highlight your ability to build production-ready mobile/web apps, optimize performance, and explain the architectural decisions you make.

questions.text: Describe a situation where you disagreed with a teammate. How did you resolve it?

answers.content: Focus on data-driven decisions and performance metrics rather than personal opinions, evaluating trade-offs calmly.

questions.text: How do you estimate development tasks? How do you prioritize your work?

answers.content: Break tasks down into smaller component-level items, estimate using complexity scales, and prioritize based on business requirements.

questions.text: Your React application is getting slow. Where do you look first?

answers.content: Look at DevTools Profiler to identify slow renders, look at bundle sizes, and inspect network logs for duplicate requests.

questions.text: A feature works perfectly in development but fails in production. How do you debug and resolve this?

answers.content: Verify environment configurations, check API CORS headers, check for optimization-induced issues (e.g. minification naming bugs), and check error logs.

questions.text: Let's have a look at a webpage. I need three API calls. Based on the responses, I populate the content on the page. I need to ensure that the page loads fast. I also need to ensure that if any API fails, I show an error message only in the corresponding block while the remaining sections continue to work. How would you implement this?

answers.content: Trigger the three API calls concurrently using Promise.allSettled() or separate queries, and wrap each component block in its own local loading/error boundary.

questions.text: How would you build a real-time dashboard displaying live data updates?

answers.content: Use WebSockets for live bidirectional updates (or Polling if sockets aren't supported). Use local throttling/debouncing to batch updates before dispatching state changes.

questions.text: Design a scalable notification system for a React application handling 1K of users up to 1M users.

answers.content: Establish websocket servers with publish-subscribe message queues (Kafka, Redis) and handle client-side rendering virtualized viewport limits.

questions.text: How would you build offline support for a social media app?

answers.content: Use local MMKV stores or databases (WatermelonDB) to cache draft items. Establish sync workers to retry network mutations when connectivity resumes.

questions.text: How do you monitor frontend applications in production?

answers.content: Integrate Sentry, LogRocket, or Datadog to capture real-time performance alerts, error dumps, and user-interaction tracking.

questions.text: What causes memory leaks in React apps? How do you detect and prevent them?

answers.content: Caused by uncleared event listeners, setInterval timers, or references to clean DOM nodes in closures. Resolved by using useEffect cleanups.
